                    <section aria-labelledby="Abs1" data-title="Abstract" lang="en"><div class="c-article-section" id="Abs1-section"><h2 id="Abs1" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item"><span class="c-article-section__title-number"> </span>Abstract</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Abs1-content"><p>In recent decades, there has been a strong trend of abandonment of traditional land uses in the Mediterranean region, leading to changes in vegetation cover and an increase in the risk of wildfires. One of the areas where anthropogenic changes in land cover have been especially prominent is the Croatian Dinaric Karst. Focusing on the last two centuries, this research contributes to the understanding of historical links between socio-economic, demographic and landscape changes that occurred in three main Dinaric socio-environmental zones (the hinterland, the littoral and the islands) and explores how they have shaped the development of fire-prone landscapes in the study region. Through a mixed-method approach, different data sources are utilised, including the analysis of existing literature, archival sources, recent comparative forestry, satellite and fieldwork data. Finally, the paper also focuses on possible future changes in the context of three development scenarios, aiming to explore how to manage and protect these landscapes at a time when both population and climate are quickly changing.</p></div></div></section>

                        <div class="main-content">
                            <section data-title="Introduction"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec1-section"><h2 id="Sec1" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">5.1 </span>Introduction</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec1-content"><p>In the last few years, the Mediterranean experienced extreme wildfires, particularly affecting South and Southeast Europe. The hardest hit areas include southern Italy, Greece, Turkey and the Croatian Dinaric Karst region in the Eastern Adriatic. The air temperature of 48.8 °C measured in Sicily on 11 August 2021 is considered the highest temperature ever measured in Europe. According to the latest IPCC report,<sup><a href="#Fn1"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>1</a></sup> the Mediterranean is a hot spot of increasing temperatures, wildfires and other related hazards. Several factors have contributed to this increase in wildfires and associated hazards, including climate change, and major land use and land cover changes over recent decades.</p><p>One of the Mediterranean areas that has experienced significant anthropogenic changes in land cover is the Croatian Dinaric Karst. The region’s sensitive environment, characterised by permeability of rock and soil and regular summer droughts, has been altered by various processes, including rapid littoralisation, agricultural abandonment, economic transition and armed conflict.</p><p>In many aspects, the Croatian Dinaric Karst, is a part of the wider Euro-Mediterranean region, both environmentally and culturally. Its position within the global atmospheric system, combined with its local topography and landforms, has contributed to the development of climate patterns that are found throughout the Mediterranean, whilst still retaining distinct local characteristics which have shaped a specific landscape structure and co-shaped a way of life. For example, regular summer droughts are a unifying feature of the Mediterranean climate, and throughout millennia, they have conditioned the development of specific agricultural practices that favour summer crops which can withstand the dry conditions, as well as arboriculture, which involves crops like the olive tree that have deep roots. Pastoralism has also played a significant role in the region, particularly in its distinctive form of transhumance, as the most convenient subsistence economy till the recent time.<sup><a href="#Fn2"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>2</a></sup>
</p><p>Throughout history, fire has played a distinctive role in maintaining this subsistence economy as well as the landscape structure of the region. However, it is important to note the difference between these controlled fires, which were purposefully used to maintain the economy and landscape structure, and uncontrolled fires that occur as a consequence of natural causes or human negligence.<sup><a href="#Fn3"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>3</a></sup> In addition to its destructive power, there is evidence that fire also plays an important role in the ecological functioning of the region.<sup><a href="#Fn4"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>4</a></sup>
</p><p>Recently, there has been a strong trend of abandonment of traditional land uses in the region, which, in line with the change of the vegetation structure and the documented climate changes, has resulted in an increased fire risk.<sup><a href="#Fn5"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>5</a></sup> This is particularly expressed in the areas of increased fuel load in the wildland–urban interface (WUI) as a consequence of de-agrarianisation and reforestation, which are further threatened by recent rising temperatures and reduced precipitation. Research shows that wildfires in WUI have recently taken on alarming dimensions in the Mediterranean countries.<sup><a href="#Fn6"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>6</a></sup></p><p>Focusing on the last two centuries, this research contributes to the understanding of the historical links between socio-economic, demographic and landscape changes that occurred in three main Dinaric socio-environmental zones: the hinterland, the littoral and the islands. The study explores how these changes have contributed to the continued development of fire-prone landscapes in the region. A mixed-method approach is utilised, incorporating different data sources such as existing literature, historical maps and narrative sources, remotely sensed images and interviews with local firefighters and farmers. Since the present state is the consequence of our past actions in and towards the environment, and the future will depend on our current actions, the paper also focuses on possible future changes through three development scenarios, aiming to explore how to manage and protect these landscapes at the time when both population and climate are quickly changing.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Croatian Dinaric Karst: Environmental History Setting"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec2-section"><h2 id="Sec2" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">5.2 </span>Croatian Dinaric Karst: Environmental History Setting</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec2-content"><p>The Dinaric Karst makes up almost half of the Croatian territory (46.6%). Environmentally, it mostly falls within the Mediterranean and sub-Mediterranean regions, characterised by corresponding climate types and patterns, vegetation and landscape structure (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig1">5.1</a>). Carbonate bedrock, mostly limestones, and karst landscapes dominate the region and condition the drainage. Coastal mountain ranges receive the highest precipitation, but most of the water disappears underground due to fractured carbonate complexes. The Mediterranean climate–ecology region encompasses the area of Mediterranean climate (Csa) in the narrow coastal belt of Dalmatia and Dalmatian islands, as well as transitional sub-Mediterranean climate (Cfa) in the hinterland and on higher mountain altitudes. The karst hydrology in Mediterranean Dinaric Croatia causes the majority of surface (precipitation) water to sink underground, leading to a significant water scarcity augmented with strong evaporation. This is particularly evident in hot summer months, when drought conditions are frequent, and during the winter, when the dry and cold wind <i>bora</i> contributes to the overall dryness. Vegetation in the region is therefore mainly composed of xerophytes, which are acclimatised to summer droughts, high temperatures and high levels of solar radiation. It consists primarily of evergreen holm oak forest (<i>Quercus ilex</i>) together with coniferous plants such as different pines (<i>Pinus</i>) and cypress (<i>Cupressus)</i> in the hottest and driest belts of littoral and islands, and sub-Mediterranean deciduous oak forest (<i>Quercus pubescens</i>), hornbeam (<i>Carpinus orientalis</i>) and beech forest (<i>Fagus sylvatica</i>) mainly in the hinterland and at higher altitudes. However, human activities such as (over)grazing, farming and logging have transformed the original natural forest into the Mediterranean and sub-Mediterranean scrubland varieties over thousands of years. Maquis is a Mediterranean scrubland biome, typically consisting of a dense growth of evergreen shrubs in the hottest and driest Mediterranean belt; on islands and in the narrow littoral zone. Sub-Mediterranean scrubland consists mostly of deciduous continental plant species, and it is mainly in the hinterland and at higher altitudes.<sup><a href="#Fn7"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>7</a></sup>
</p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-1" data-title="Fig. 5.1"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig1" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 5.1</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><a class="c-article-section__figure-link" data-test="img-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="image" data-track-action="view figure" href="/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5/figures/1" rel="nofollow"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/chp%3A10.1007%2F978-3-031-56089-7_5/MediaObjects/500207_1_En_5_Fig1_HTML.png?as=webp"><img aria-describedby="Fig1" src="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/chp%3A10.1007%2F978-3-031-56089-7_5/MediaObjects/500207_1_En_5_Fig1_HTML.png" alt="A map of the Croatian Dinaric Karst region in which the case study areas of Vis, Sibenik and Svilaja are highlighted by a bounding box." loading="lazy" width="685" height="529"></picture></a><p class="c-article-section__figure-credit text-right c-article-section__figure-credit-right" data-test="figure-credit"><i>Source</i> Authors’ own elaboration, data source: The area and approximate northern border of the Dinaric Karst in Croatia according to Roglić<span class="unsupported-element u-hide">Footnote</span>
                        </p><p>Roglić (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1965" title="" href="#ref-CR115" id="ref-link-section-d7342104e861">1965</a>), pp. 79–87; Roglić (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1974" title="" href="#ref-CR116" id="ref-link-section-d7342104e864">1974</a>), pp. 1–69.</p>
                       and Gams<span class="unsupported-element u-hide">Footnote</span>
                        <p>Gams (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1974" title="" href="#ref-CR82" id="ref-link-section-d7342104e873">1974</a>), p. 359; Gams (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2004" title="" href="#ref-CR83" id="ref-link-section-d7342104e876">2004</a>), p. 27.</p>
                      
<p></p></div><div class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-1-desc"><p>Schematic map of the socio-environmental zones of the Croatian Dinaric Karst and the location of the case study areas.</p></div></div><div class="u-text-right u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="chapter-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5/figures/1" data-track-dest="link:Figure1 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 1" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div>
<p>For centuries, the population of the Dinaric Karst region has relied heavily on pastoralism as a convenient subsistence economy and a way of life,<sup><a href="#Fn10"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>10</a></sup> adapting to the region’s climate constraints and karst environment, which are characterised by scarce water, soil, and arable land.<sup><a href="#Fn11"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>11</a></sup> Of the other economic activities, agriculture, logging and fuelwood gathering, together with pastoralism, had the greatest impact on the land.<sup><a href="#Fn12"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>12</a></sup> The basic structure of the Mediterranean rural landscape has been defined by French geographers,<sup><a href="#Fn13"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>13</a></sup> using a Roman trilogy of general land use—the <i>ager</i>, which consisted of both seeds (arable farming) and trees (arboriculture); outside these arable areas, which are highly localised in the Dinaric Karst, is the <i>saltus</i>, i.e. the scrubland used for grazing; and the forest—<i>silva</i>, which was fragile as it was constantly threatened by shepherds or loggers.</p><p>There is ample evidence of forest clearing and burning throughout history. Although anthropogenic pressure in the Dinaric Karst region can be traced back to millennia, most authors believe that the process of deforestation, primarily associated with (over)grazing but also with other land uses, began intensively in the fourteenth century.<sup><a href="#Fn14"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>14</a></sup> Although there have been examples of sustainable management of resources,<sup><a href="#Fn15"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>15</a></sup> many cultivation techniques were untenable due to political insecurity and frequent wars which were particularly evident in the Croatian Dinaric Karst, a combat zone and frontier for centuries.<sup><a href="#Fn16"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>16</a></sup> This led to ignorance of laws and agreements, ultimately resulting in rapid depletion of forest or overgrazing of pastures. The pastoral economy in the Mediterranean has always tended towards overgrazing, which haunted the landscapes for centuries.<sup><a href="#Fn17"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>17</a></sup>
</p><p>Fire played an important role in maintaining <i>saltus</i> and pastures by preventing them from reverting to forests and promoting grassland regeneration. Post-fire plants have a much higher mineral and protein content (as much as 300–700%), and these nutritional properties, together with the ash salts, were important for the quality of feed for grazing animals.<sup><a href="#Fn18"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>18</a></sup> This was a common practice of the cattle breeders, which was also known in other European regions,<sup><a href="#Fn19"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>19</a></sup> but the costs of pastoralism in the fragile Mediterranean mountain ecosystem were far higher than similar practices in northern and southern Europe.<sup><a href="#Fn20"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>20</a></sup>
</p><p>According to cadastral<sup><a href="#Fn21"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>21</a></sup> and narrative sources<sup><a href="#Fn22"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>22</a></sup> from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, it appears that overgrazing in this fragile, sensitive Mediterranean karst environment had negative impact, ultimately leading to deforestation and unsustainable grassland use. As a result, the landscape was perceived as barren, dry and rocky, with little vegetation. In contrast, more humid hinterland mountains were perceived as green islands in the midst of a rocky desert.<sup><a href="#Fn23"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>23</a></sup>
</p><p>The special distinctiveness of Croatian Dinaric Karst lies in its longitudinal zonation (NW–SE direction). This zonation is reflected not only in the environmental factors, including geomorphology, climate and vegetation, but also in the cultural and ecological contexts. This interplay between the environmental zonation and human influences co-affects the way of life and subsistence economy. The Croatian Dinaric Karst features three distinct zones, ranging from the hottest and driest Euro-Mediterranean belt to the sub-Mediterranean. These zones include the island belt, the littoral and the hinterland (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig1">5.1</a>).</p><p>The Eastern Adriatic littoral has maintained a degree of continuity since Antiquity, with urban and economic networks developing with Greek poleis in the central Adriatic, and later with Roman and mediaeval Croatian cities along the entire coast. This long-term characteristic of the Littoral has persisted despite significant changes over time. Although the level of connection between the littoral and the hinterland has varied over history, it has remained relatively strong for the most part. However, the configuration and longitudinal zonation of Croatian Dinaric Karst—with its high mountain barrier to the hinterland—have contributed to the hinterland remaining peripheral in relation to the main littoral development fluxes. As a result, the hinterland has primarily developed as remote, peripheral rural areas.<sup><a href="#Fn24"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>24</a></sup>
</p><p>In the second half of the twentieth century, the process of intense littoralisation brought significant economic and demographic growth to the littoral zone, mostly due to the tourism and related industries. The demographic progress in the littoral zone is directly dependent on population outflow from the hinterland and islands—two other rural marginal zones—which served as the workforce reservoir for the expanding economic activities in the littoral. Such a massive population outflow resulted in the dissolution of a traditional lifestyle that was centred around pastoralism and localised tillage zones in the karst. As a consequence, there was widespread land abandonment and considerable environmental change, primarily expressed through vegetation succession. These landscape changes directly influence the fire risk. Our research, as well as some previous findings for other Mediterranean areas, shows that the wildfire risk is closely related to land cover,<sup><a href="#Fn25"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>25</a></sup> whilst it is also linked to some societal factors, such as the loss of traditional knowledge of fire management due to depopulation.<sup><a href="#Fn26"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>26</a></sup>
</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Research Overview"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec3-section"><h2 id="Sec3" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">5.3 </span>Research Overview</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec3-content"><p>The characteristics of fire regimes in the Mediterranean have been the topic of considerable research in recent decades.<sup><a href="#Fn27"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>27</a></sup> Many of these studies point out the complexity of the issue of wildfires, with much of the debate centring on the relative contribution of climate and fuel (i.e. natural vegetation cover available for combustion). This issue has been studied through a range of case studies across the Mediterranean, attracting strong arguments from both sides.<sup><a href="#Fn28"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>28</a></sup> Hill<sup><a href="#Fn29"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>29</a></sup> argued that the ‘syndrome’ of rural exodus and land abandonment has been a major contributing factor to the increased fire hazards in all  Mediterranean countries, with the exception of coastal regions where tourism and urbanisation dominate. Pausas and Keeley<sup><a href="#Fn30"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>30</a></sup> have also concluded that the reduction of agriculture, grazing and controlled fires due to the depopulation of rural areas has led to fuel build-up. This, coupled with increased ignitions at the wildland–urban interface, has caused an increase in large high-intensity fires. Other studies also emphasise that land use and land management changes are the Mediterranean fire regime.<sup><a href="#Fn31"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>31</a></sup>
</p><p>On the other hand, it has been established that some of the annual variability in burned area can be explained by climatic parameters,<sup><a href="#Fn32"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>32</a></sup> whilst others stress the interplay of both climatic and non-climatic factors. Turco et al.<sup><a href="#Fn33"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>33</a></sup> conducted a quantitative assessment of climate, environmental and socio-economic changes since the 1970s and concluded that positive trends in fire frequency can be explained by both recent socio-economic transformations and climate warming in recent decades. In a comprehensive study that included data on the 130-year fire history in the Spanish province of Valencia,<sup><a href="#Fn34"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>34</a></sup> fire occurrence data were correlated with rural population censuses and climate data. The results have indicated that a major shift in the fire regime happened in Spain in the 1970s due to the accumulation of fuel resulting from decades of land abandonment. However, data showed that after the massive fires in the 1970s, there was a stronger correlation between climate parameters and fire occurrence than with socio-economic changes. In another study,<sup><a href="#Fn35"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>35</a></sup> the fire regime data for the agriculturally developed Rif region in north Morocco were compared with the Valencian one prior to the 1970s shift, when the traditional rural economy collapsed, and the fire regime became fuel-limited. The findings indicated that the current fire regime in the Rif matches the pre-1970s fire regime observed in Valencia.</p><p>In addition to the study of fire regimes, different studies have also analysed the susceptibility of different land cover types to fires. For instance, research<sup><a href="#Fn36"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>36</a></sup> concluded that in Mediterranean Europe, scrublands and conifer stands are more prone to large fires, whilst agricultural areas are less susceptible. This has been confirmed by Barros and Pereira<sup><a href="#Fn37"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>37</a></sup> who showed that fire selectivity is higher for scrublands, pine stands and eucalyptus plantations compared to agricultural crops and agroforestry lands. Similarly, Moreira et al.<sup><a href="#Fn38"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>38</a></sup> found that scrublands were the only land cover type that burned much more than expected. Finally, the preference of fire for a specific land cover type changes with the size of the fire, with the effect diminishing as the size of the fire increases.<sup><a href="#Fn39"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>39</a></sup>
</p><p>Whilst recent research on fire regimes focuses on the period since the 1970s, when Earth observation satellites became available for quick and efficient tracking of global and regional coverage of fire occurrences,<sup><a href="#Fn40"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>40</a></sup> a longer historical perspective is often needed to fully understand changes in these regimes. In Croatia, research on this topic is still relatively underdeveloped, and much of it has been based on analysing the characteristics and spatial distribution of contemporary fires. For instance, Pavlek et al.<sup><a href="#Fn41"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>41</a></sup> analysed environmental and socio-economic factors that influence fire occurrence in Mediterranean Croatia in 2013 and concluded that large fires correlated with scrubland and other types of degraded vegetation which highlights the importance of socio-economic and demographic processes such as depopulation and de-ruralisation for the fire regime. A similar conclusion was reached by Jajtić et al.<sup><a href="#Fn42"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>42</a></sup> when comparing the fire seasons of 2011 and 2013. Mamut<sup><a href="#Fn43"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>43</a></sup> confirmed the importance of vegetation cover for fire risk in the period from 1998 to 2008, but also stressed the importance of the Mediterranean climate and particularly dominant winds.</p><p>The long-term historical perspective of the relationship between environmental changes and fire risk in the Croatian Dinaric Karst is mainly studied by Cvitanović, Durbešić, Fuerst-Bjeliš and Tekić<sup><a href="#Fn44"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>44</a></sup> for the hinterland and littoral regions of the Eastern Adriatic. Their findings indicate that changes in subsistence farming over the last two centuries have contributed to an increase in fire risk. Specifically, land abandonment has led to vegetation succession, resulting in an increase in the most fire-prone vegetation cover types such as sub-Mediterranean scrub and evergreen forest.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Scope and Methodology"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec4-section"><h2 id="Sec4" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">5.4 </span>Scope and Methodology</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec4-content"><p>To investigate the interdependence between fire risk in the Croatian Dinaric Karst area and the landscape changes resulting from socio-economic processes and climate change, three distinct case studies have been analysed through two comparative periods—the nineteenth century and the present. The case studies were chosen to represent three zones of Croatian Dinaric Karst, each marked by different environmental conditions and socio-economic development through history. The littoral zone, situated along the Eastern Adriatic littoral development axis, encompasses an area in close proximity to the city of Šibenik. This zone serves as a prime example of a semi-urbanised coastal landscape that has transitioned from an economy based on wine and olive oil production to one focused on tourism. It also maintains strong connections with the nearby urban centre. The hinterland zone, centred around Svilaja mountain, is characterised by a rural, agro-pastoral landscape. Lastly, the island socio-environmental zone is represented by Vis island, one of the more remote and sparsely populated islands in the region. Due to its isolation, the island has been able to retain its traditional islander lifestyle for a longer period (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig1">5.1</a>). Each case study was assessed through analysis and comparison of historical records from the nineteenth century and contemporary data on land use, land cover and climate, which was followed by the calculation of the fire risk for both periods.</p><p>The selection of parameters for fire risk assessment is defined by the Ministry of the Internal Affairs of Croatia and is provided by the official Regulation on the Forest Fire Protection (2014)<sup><a href="#Fn45"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>45</a></sup> and Fire Risk assessment measures (2003).<sup><a href="#Fn46"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>46</a></sup> Each parameter is evaluated and assigned a score based on its potential fire risk. Factors such as land cover and land use data, climate parameters and anthropogenic factors are considered variable and can change over time. Other parameters such as lithological characteristics, soil, relief and exposure are assumed to be constant in this analysis. Based on these assessment documents, the riskiest parameters include coniferous forests and degraded forests due to their high resin content and dryness; forests near arable land where weeds are frequently burned; and recreational areas such as wildland–urban interface (WUI). Additionally, areas with high mean annual temperature, low mean annual precipitation and low humidity also pose a higher fire risk, as do rock layers of sands, limestone or dolomite; southern exposure; low elevation; and low forest structure.</p><p>This research made use of detailed nineteenth-century cadastral plans and accompanying documentation gathered during the Franciscan cadastral survey of Dalmatia between 1823 and 1838, which provided comprehensive land use data for the area. These data were organised according to administrative sections called communes, which corresponded to the territory of individual settlements. To conduct a thorough analysis of the land use categories, the cadastral plans were digitised. This was accompanied by an analysis of narrative historical sources that provided contextual information to complement the data. For contemporary land use and land cover, a combination of sources was used, including CLCCro (Corine Land Cover) Datasets, management programmes for management units provided by Croatian Forests Ltd<sup><a href="#Fn47"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>47</a></sup> and interpretation of landscape through satellite imagery and fieldwork assessment.</p><p>To enable a valid and clear comparison of land use and land cover between the two periods, adjustment and unification (merger) of the landscape categories were necessary due to the different sources used for evaluation. The sources varied in their type, methodology and origin (cadastre, CLCCro, forestry documentation, fieldwork). To achieve this, the study defined fewer main landscape categories (instead of the more detailed categories used in the nineteenth-century cadastre) that are relevant for fire risk assessment. These categories include forest (evergreen, deciduous), scrubland (maquis and sub-Mediterranean), pastures, arable land (including olive groves) and vineyards. In the nineteenth-century cadastral records, scrubland/maquis was not present as a land use category but was included in the forest category ‘<i>bosco di stanghe’</i> or forest with scrubland, whilst the categories ‘<i>young forest’</i>, ‘<i>forest with mid-sized trees’</i> and ‘<i>forests with tall trunks’</i> were included in the forest category. In contrast, pastures were those land parcels where the main activity was animal grazing and were marked with prevalence of grassy vegetation, although woody vegetation in the form of shrubs may have been present. The category of ‘pasture’ for modern period taken from CLCCro Dataset also implies existence of shrubs and woody vegetation, but it had to be covering < 30% of the ground. All other categories, such as settlements, roads and waters, that are not relevant for fire risk and/or cover only small sections of study areas are included in the category ‘other’.</p><p>Climate parameters were obtained from the Croatian Meteorological and Hydrological Service. Given the limited data available for the nineteenth century, we relied on the meteorological station of Hvar, which recorded temperature, precipitation and humidity from 1858 to 1888. Due to the territorial proximity of all case studies to this station (25 km from Vis island, and approximately 65 km from the city of Šibenik and Svilaja mountain areas: Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig1">5.1</a>), it represents a valid source for average temperature, precipitation and humidity values, key climate parameters for assessing the fire risk. Due to the higher elevation of Svilaja mountain, the temperature gradient was taken into consideration and data corrected accordingly.</p><p>In the course of a previous study, three scenarios of spatial development were constructed for the region of Croatian Dinaric Karst (Dalmatia), covering the period until 2031. Thereby, results of multivariate statistical analysis (factor and cluster analysis) were used to isolate underlying factors of development characteristics and develop a regional typology. These results were then combined with two rounds of the Delphi method, where an interdisciplinary panel of experts examined possible paths for the future development of Dalmatia and its subregions. The resulting scenarios showed processes leading from the contemporary situation towards a future state, meaning that they had explorative character.<sup><a href="#Fn48"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>48</a></sup> In this study, the research team used these scenarios as a framework to explore how socio-economic, demographic and landscape changes could influence the wildfire incidence in the three main Dinaric socio-environmental zones: the hinterland, the littoral and the islands.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Results and Discussion"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec5-section"><h2 id="Sec5" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">5.5 </span>Results and Discussion</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec5-content"><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec6"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">5.5.1 </span>Landscape Change Since the Nineteenth Century</h3><p>According to travel accounts from the eighteenth century, the Croatian Dinaric Karst landscape was predominantly treeless and dotted with cultivated valleys that were nestled between the barren hills. These descriptions have been corroborated by detailed statistical data on land use in the late eighteenth century.<sup><a href="#Fn49"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>49</a></sup> The available historical data on the economy of the region confirm that agriculture and especially pastoralism were the primary means of livelihood. As agricultural density increased over time, this led to greater pressure on the landscape. Woodlands in particular were affected, with frequent cutting of firewood and poorly regulated<sup><a href="#Fn50"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>50</a></sup> or even sustainable<sup><a href="#Fn51"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>51</a></sup> agroforestry practices, but also by flocks of sheep and goats for grazing contributing to their decline.<sup><a href="#Fn52"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>52</a></sup> Given the poor quality of karst pastures, woodlands played a crucial role in sustaining the region’s sheep and goat populations. During harsh periods, the leaves, buds and small branches of trees offered a vital source of food. As a result, the history of pastoralism in the Croatian Dinaric Karst is closely linked to the loss of woodlands, as the need for grazing land and fodder drove the clearing and conversion of forested areas. The cadastral survey of the Austrian Empire, carried out in Dalmatia between 1823 and 1838, provides the most detailed and precise information on land use in the nineteenth century. Woodland areas were abundant on the islands of southern Dalmatia, where the shipbuilding industry mandated strict regulations for their preservation.<sup><a href="#Fn53"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>53</a></sup> On the mainland, they covered the sparsely populated hilly and semi-mountainous areas in the hinterland. In contrast, the coastal zone was characterised by a pronounced lack of forests, reflecting the increased pressure on the landscape due to high population density and economic development. However, it should be noted that in Dalmatia, there was a lack of proper forests with older and developed trees. As an Austrian official from the late eighteenth century described it, most ‘forest’ was ‘scrubland rather than forest, bushes rather than trees’.<sup><a href="#Fn54"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>54</a></sup>
</p><p>Cadastral records for three case studies clearly emphasise the prevalent landscape categories (Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="#Tab1">5.1</a>; Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig2">5.2</a>). Pastures were the most dominant land use category in the littoral and hinterland areas, covering 83% (Šibenik—littoral) and 67% (Svilaja—hinterland) of the area, respectively. This reflects the centuries-old lifestyle of the communities living in the area, which has developed as an adaptation to the climate and karst characteristics of the region, such as lack of water, lack of arable land and regular summer drought. The category of pastures includes several subcategories, such as pastures with bushes, pastures with coppiced trees and pastures with vineyards/olive/fruit trees. According to cadastral records, these areas were used for livestock grazing and unsupervised firewood collection, indicating the prevalence of an open-type landscape with some elements of maquis/sub-Mediterranean scrubland, but not in continuous cover. On Vis island, pastures covered 29% of the area, whilst maquis was the most widespread category with a share of almost 50%. This reflects the fact that Vis was the furthest populated island from the coast, and its relatively small population placed more emphasis on shipbuilding, fishing and viticulture. Forests as a class were significantly present only in the hinterland socio-environmental zone (case study Svilaja mountain) where they covered 17% of the area.</p><div class="c-article-table" data-test="inline-table" data-container-section="table" id="table-1"><figure><figcaption class="c-article-table__figcaption"><b id="Tab1" data-test="table-caption">Table 5.1 Land use categories in the nineteenth century</b></figcaption><div class="u-text-right u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="table-link" data-track="click" data-track-action="view table" data-track-label="button" rel="nofollow" href="/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5/tables/1" aria-label="Full size table 1"><span>Full size table</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div>
<div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-2" data-title="Fig. 5.2"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig2" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 5.2</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><a class="c-article-section__figure-link" data-test="img-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="image" data-track-action="view figure" href="/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5/figures/2" rel="nofollow"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/chp%3A10.1007%2F978-3-031-56089-7_5/MediaObjects/500207_1_En_5_Fig2_HTML.png?as=webp"><img aria-describedby="Fig2" src="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/chp%3A10.1007%2F978-3-031-56089-7_5/MediaObjects/500207_1_En_5_Fig2_HTML.png" alt="Three pie charts each of the land use categories in the nineteenth and twenty first centuries for Littoral, Island and Hinterland. Pastures were the most dominant land use category in the littoral and hinterland areas, covering 83% and 67%, respectively. Scrublands were the most dominant land use in the littoral and hinterland areas, covering 31.4% and 43.5%, respectively" loading="lazy" width="685" height="627"></picture></a><p class="c-article-section__figure-credit text-right c-article-section__figure-credit-right" data-test="figure-credit"><i>Source</i> Authors’ own elaboration, data source: Tables <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="#Tab1">5.1</a> and <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="#Tab2">5.2</a></p></div><div class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-2-desc"><p>Land use categories in the nineteenth and twenty-first centuries.</p></div></div><div class="u-text-right u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="chapter-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5/figures/2" data-track-dest="link:Figure2 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 2" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div>
<p>Agricultural activities have been declining in Croatia throughout the whole twentieth century, but the process intensified especially after the Second World War. Rural emigration was emphasised by the rapid industrialisation of the littoral and the development of tourism there. The decline of agricultural activities in Croatia began in the twentieth century and was further intensified after the Second World War. The planned development of industry in the coastal region, coupled with the growth of tourism, led to a shift in focus from the islands and hinterland to the coast.<sup><a href="#Fn56"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>56</a></sup> This process of littoralisation resulted in rural emigration, a collapse of pastoralism and a decrease in the share of the agricultural population in Dalmatia from 72.1% in 1948 to just 3.4% in 1991.<sup><a href="#Fn57"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>57</a></sup> The availability of employment outside agriculture was a contributing factor to this decline. Although some exploitation of woodlands by the local people continued until the 1990s, the scale of it was insignificant compared to the earlier periods. The Croatian War of Independence further contributed to rural abandonment, particularly in the hinterland. Extensive land abandonment led to rapid vegetation succession, with open areas quickly being overgrown by pine trees that spread from plantations through wind-dispersed seeds.</p><p>The impacts of economic and demographic changes on land use in Croatia are clearly visible in the land use categories of 2021 (Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="#Tab2">5.2</a>; Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig2">5.2</a>). In the hinterland, pastures have decreased considerably to only 32% of the total area, whilst sub-Mediterranean scrubland has increased to 43%. This reflects the process of rural abandonment and vegetation succession, which has primarily affected areas historically used for grazing, as the share of arable land has not decreased significantly. The emergence of evergreen forest with almost 6% of land cover in the hinterland is due to reforestation efforts, where black pine (<i>Pinus nigra</i>) was planted in order to prevent slope erosion and floods. Littoral areas have experienced dramatic decreases in the coverage of pastures, which have decreased from 82% to just 27% of the land area. This process of succession has resulted in an increase in maquis to almost 15% of the area and sub-Mediterranean scrubland to over 31%, whilst arable land increased by almost 6%. Similar to the hinterland area, the emergence of evergreen forest is attributed to extensive reforestation efforts that established pine monocultures throughout the twentieth century with the difference being that <i>Pinus halepensis</i> was the dominant pine species planted here. <i>Pinus halepensis</i> now covers almost 40% of the wider Šibenik area with dense stands, whilst a further 40% is covered with sparse formations. This is a yearly increase of 600% from 170 years ago when only a single stand was present on the island of Krapanj.<sup><a href="#Fn58"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>58</a></sup> The decline of vineyards on the islands and in the littoral is a direct result of depopulation and de-agrarianisation;<sup><a href="#Fn59"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>59</a></sup> however, the lower resolution of the twenty-first century land use maps, compared to detailed cadastral survey from the nineteenth century, has led to an exclusion of very small parcels with vineyards which makes viticulture underrepresented in the twenty-first-century statistics.</p><div class="c-article-table" data-test="inline-table" data-container-section="table" id="table-2"><figure><figcaption class="c-article-table__figcaption"><b id="Tab2" data-test="table-caption">Table 5.2 Land use categories in the twenty-first century</b></figcaption><div class="u-text-right u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="table-link" data-track="click" data-track-action="view table" data-track-label="button" rel="nofollow" href="/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5/tables/2" aria-label="Full size table 2"><span>Full size table</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div>
<h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec7"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">5.5.2 </span>Fire Risk Assessment and Change in the Course of Two Centuries: From the Nineteenth to Twenty-First Century</h3><p>Fire risk for all three case studies was evaluated according to the Croatian methodology established by the official <i>Fire risk assessment measures</i> (2003). The parameters of lithology, pedology, orography and exposure were considered constant and did not change between comparative periods, whilst climate, anthropogenic factors and especially vegetation cover represent changing variables that directly influence the changing fire risk vulnerability. According to the official <i>Fire risk assessment measures</i>, the relevant climate parameters for fire risk assessment are mean temperature, precipitation and humidity. To compare the values between different periods, we measured the change in climate parameters between 1858–1888 and 1991–2018<sup><a href="#Fn61"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>61</a></sup> at the Hvar station. This station was selected as the only representative station for the study areas due to the availability of data for the nineteenth century (as described in the Scope and Methodology section). Between the two comparison periods, mean temperature increased by 0.9 °C, mean precipitation decreased by 17.5 mm, whilst mean air humidity remained constant at 66%. The observed increase in temperature and decrease in precipitation are generally consistent with climate change in the Mediterranean region, and both contribute to the increased fire risk.</p><p>To estimate the values of the nineteenth century for all case studies and respective socio-environmental zones, we applied the determined values of change to other meteorological stations in the study area. Specifically, we used the Knin meteorological station for the hinterland, the Šibenik station for the littoral area of Šibenik and the Komiža station on the island of Vis. Despite the observed increase in temperature and decrease in precipitation, which generally leads to higher fire risk, our analysis suggests that these changes in climate parameters are not the most critical factors for increased fire risk. This is because all corresponding values of climate parameters were already in the highest category of fire risk assessment (mean <i>T</i> above 12 °C and mean precipitation below 800 mm) in the nineteenth century, with the exception of slightly higher mean precipitation in the hinterland (station Knin and Svilaja mountain; mean precipitation above 1000 mm), which may reduce overall fire risk.</p><p>In the nineteenth century, pastures dominated the mainland landscape, with a low share of either forest or degraded forms of forest such as scrubland or maquis. This open type of landscape was mostly characterised by medium fire risk in 91% of the area in the littoral case study and 83% of the area in the hinterland. However, the island of Vis had almost 70% of the area under high fire risk, mostly due to the larger share of maquis, which is proven to be the most fire-prone vegetation type,<sup><a href="#Fn62"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>62</a></sup> and a lower share of open pastures in comparison with the mainland (Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="#Tab3">5.3</a>; Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig3">5.3</a>).</p><div class="c-article-table" data-test="inline-table" data-container-section="table" id="table-3"><figure><figcaption class="c-article-table__figcaption"><b id="Tab3" data-test="table-caption">Table 5.3 Fire risk assessment in the nineteenth century</b></figcaption><div class="u-text-right u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="table-link" data-track="click" data-track-action="view table" data-track-label="button" rel="nofollow" href="/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5/tables/3" aria-label="Full size table 3"><span>Full size table</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div>
<div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-3" data-title="Fig. 5.3"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig3" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 5.3</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><a class="c-article-section__figure-link" data-test="img-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="image" data-track-action="view figure" href="/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5/figures/3" rel="nofollow"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/chp%3A10.1007%2F978-3-031-56089-7_5/MediaObjects/500207_1_En_5_Fig3_HTML.png?as=webp"><img aria-describedby="Fig3" src="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/chp%3A10.1007%2F978-3-031-56089-7_5/MediaObjects/500207_1_En_5_Fig3_HTML.png" alt="Three pie charts each of the fire risk assessment in the nineteenth and twenty first centuries for Littoral, Island and Hinterland. There is a medium fire risk were the most dominant in the littoral and hinterland areas, covering 91.3% and 83.2%, respectively. High fire risk were the most dominant land use in the littoral and hinterland areas, covering 70.8% and 53.6%, respectively" loading="lazy" width="685" height="684"></picture></a><p class="c-article-section__figure-credit text-right c-article-section__figure-credit-right" data-test="figure-credit"><i>Source</i> Authors’ own elaboration, data source: Tables <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="#Tab3">5.3</a> and <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="#Tab4">5.4</a></p></div><div class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-3-desc"><p>Fire risk assessment in the nineteenth and twenty-first centuries.</p></div></div><div class="u-text-right u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="chapter-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5/figures/3" data-track-dest="link:Figure3 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 3" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div>
<p>The increase of fire risk observed in the twentieth and twenty-first century in all case studies is closely linked to landscape changes that occurred in the twentieth century, specifically, the succession of vegetation types of maquis and garrigue on former pastures. The share of the category of high fire risk in the twenty-first century has increased to 53% in the hinterland, 70% in the coastal area and to 92% on the Vis island. The data for the island of Vis, although indicative, should be viewed with caution as there are no official government data (Croatian Forests Ltd) on land use in private ownership for the twenty-first century. The share of land use in private ownership amounting to 63.83% of the total area was assessed through analysis and calculation from the Corine Land Cover Dataset (CLCCro 2021).The ratio of moderate to high risk in the hinterland is more favourable compared to the other case studies due to the beneficial effect of orography (higher elevation and related higher mean precipitation), as well as the lack of human impact due to heavy depopulation and the absence of agricultural burning in the second half of the twentieth century (Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="#Tab4">5.4</a>; Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="#Fig3">5.3</a>).</p><div class="c-article-table" data-test="inline-table" data-container-section="table" id="table-4"><figure><figcaption class="c-article-table__figcaption"><b id="Tab4" data-test="table-caption">Table 5.4 Fire risk assessment in the twenty-first century</b></figcaption><div class="u-text-right u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="table-link" data-track="click" data-track-action="view table" data-track-label="button" rel="nofollow" href="/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5/tables/4" aria-label="Full size table 4"><span>Full size table</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div>
<p>According to recent research,<sup><a href="#Fn65"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>65</a></sup> wildfires in the Croatian Dinaric Karst show similar patterns to other Mediterranean areas, primarily in the north and west, where there has been a rapid increase in burned area in the second half of the twentieth century. However, the southern and eastern Mediterranean has experienced relatively lower levels of fire activity, possibly due to different patterns of land use (overgrazing and high pressure on forest in terms of subsistence clear-cutting).<sup><a href="#Fn66"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>66</a></sup>
</p><p>From 1958 to 1967, an average of 2407 ha of woodland area burned each year in Croatia, and this increased to 3685 ha in 1968 and to almost 5000 ha in the 1980s.<sup><a href="#Fn67"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>67</a></sup> Most of these fires took place in the Dinaric Karst during the summer months. As depopulation and land abandonment continued to intensify in the 1990s, because of general economic and social changes that were further emphasised by the Croatian War of Independence (1991–1995), forest fires became even more problematic.</p><p>More detailed research focusing on types of vegetation and contributing factors of fire occurrence in littoral counties in Croatia shows that scrubland and grasslands in the Croatian Dinaric Karst (Dalmatian region) are characterised by both a large number of fires and a large total area burned, although the fires are smaller on average on a statistically significant level,<sup><a href="#Fn68"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>68</a></sup> which is consistent with other Mediterranean areas.<sup><a href="#Fn69"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>69</a></sup> On the other hand, forests have a lower number of fires overall, but the burned area tends to be 3–4 times larger than the average.</p><p>The connection between wildfire occurrence on one side and grassland and scrubland vegetation cover on the other is usually explained through agricultural abandonment, which resulted in an accumulation of surface fuel.<sup><a href="#Fn70"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>70</a></sup> Additionally, grassland and scrubland can also be seen as highly intermingled vegetation types at different stages of the process of agricultural abandonment and secondary succession. Interviews with firefighters and farmers in the area have also confirmed the links between the occurrence of wildfires and the process of agricultural abandonment.<sup><a href="#Fn71"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>71</a></sup>
</p><p>Whilst the link between population changes and agricultural abandonment is evident, establishing a direct link between population change and fire occurrence has proven more challenging. Research has highlighted a connection between fire occurrence and a general decline in population, but only in rural areas with a significant share of the agricultural population.<sup><a href="#Fn72"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>72</a></sup> The research on forest fires causes and motivations in the South and Southeast Europe, including Croatia, has shown that agricultural burnings are the most prevalent cause of forest fires; most of them stem from negligence.<sup><a href="#Fn73"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>73</a></sup> It seems that traditional agricultural practices of burning agricultural waste and old grass are not a useful wildfire prevention method anymore, likely due to an overall increase in vegetation cover which represents easily flammable fuel.<sup><a href="#Fn74"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>74</a></sup> The advanced age of farmers practising this management method together with the loss of traditional knowledge could play a role as well. Some research, although inconclusive and spatially variable, suggests that this might be also a consequence of climate change which changed the patterns of days suitable for adapted agricultural burning, either moving them to earlier spring and later autumn months, or reducing them overall.<sup><a href="#Fn75"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>75</a></sup>
</p><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec8"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">5.5.3 </span>Wildland–Urban Interface: Potential New Fire Risk Areas?</h3><p>Urbanisation, peri-urbanisation and littoralisation, coupled with tourism and recreation, have intensified human activities in environments that are increasingly prone to wildfires due to the abandonment of traditional farming practices. All this, together with the widespread afforestation with pine trees along the coast, contributes significantly to the increase in fire risk.</p><p>The littoral zone of the Croatian Dinaric Karst is a development axis, attracting economic activities and population mainly from the hinterland and the island zone. This has led to the creation of wildland–urban interface (WUI) zones that represent new fire risk areas due to the combination of land abandonment and the proliferation of scrubland and maquis vegetation. These conditions result in a concentration of fuel, along with increasing peri-urban and recreational activities, which increase the risk of fire. The expansion of WUI zones has been a global trend in recent decades and has a direct relationship with the risk of forest fires, as human activities increase the likelihood of ignition and the spread of wildfires.<sup><a href="#Fn76"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>76</a></sup> The map of WUI areas in Europe suggests that the trend of urban growth in the Croatian Dinaric Karst is still only moderate in comparison with other Mediterranean regions. In addition, the correlation of large fires with the extent of WUI shows that large fires occur slightly less frequently near WUI areas here than away from WUI areas, but the difference is not statistically significant.<sup><a href="#Fn77"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>77</a></sup> However, recent research in the Croatian Dinaric Karst has identified that areas in close vicinity to the largest littoral cities of Zadar, Šibenik, Split and Dubrovnik are indeed at a higher risk of fire occurrence,<sup><a href="#Fn78"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>78</a></sup> pointing to the increasing importance of WUI.</p><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec9"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">5.5.4 </span>Moving Forward: Wildfire Risk Within the Scope of Development Scenarios</h3><p>Without knowing and understanding the relationships between humans and the environment in the past, we are unable to understand the current state of the environment and its processes, including the risk of wildfires. On the other hand, if we know and understand the past and present of our actions and human–environment relationships, we can use this knowledge to predict and possibly (re)manage undesirable and unsustainable developments in the future.</p><p>Three development scenarios for Dalmatia, as a region of Croatian Dinaric Karst, and its subregions examine possible future developments from different perspectives: ‘Monoculture of tourism’ (MoT), ‘Sustainable tourism’ (ST) and ‘Integral development’ (ID).<sup><a href="#Fn79"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>79</a></sup> In the MoT scenario, tourism exclusively dominates the economic and employment structure of Dalmatia, with high seasonal activity. To a limited degree, tourism development is tied with local agriculture, and to a higher degree with complementary manufacturing, services and the construction sector. It is also followed by infrastructural development, but levels of environmental protection, as well as innovation and technology, will be low. Tourism will not help in reversing depopulation and population ageing. The population will continue concentrating in the coastal zone, whereby hinterland and islands will be used as secondary, ‘weekend’ places of residence.</p><p>In the ST scenario, tourism supply is highly diversified, with strong effects on the development of agriculture, manufacturing, small-scale industries, trade and various services. Compared to the monoculture of tourism, the institutional framework will be stronger and levels of knowledge and innovation higher. A higher degree of employment and economic activities will still be connected with bigger cities, spreading in the cities’ surroundings. Infrastructural development will, along with the increasing role of smaller- and middle-sized urban centres, influence more balanced and spatially dispersed development. Smaller towns on the coastline, as well as islands and the hinterland, will experience an increasingly seasonal way of living.</p><p>The ID scenario examines development based on reindustrialisation. Knowledge, innovation, information and communication technologies, and technological development in general, will bring about the increased significance of production sectors, similar to the level of importance held prior to the 1990s, before the political–economic change and the 1991–1995 Croatian War of Independence took place. In some parts of Dalmatia, tourism will remain the most important economic activity. Complementary development of agriculture and tourism will contribute to the overall development of islands and the hinterland. Although demographic ageing will remain a major issue throughout the region, new year-round job opportunities will influence the migration of highly educated workers. In parts of the hinterland and the more easily accessible islands, depopulation will decrease.<sup><a href="#Fn80"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>80</a></sup>
</p><p>As explained previously in the chapter, several main factors were recognised as possible influences in the wildfire incidence. Within the framework of each scenario, the level of risk could increase/decrease in the period until 2031 or remain unchanged. It is also expected that the risk level will differ amongst the three socio-environmental zones (Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="#Tab5">5.5</a>).</p><div class="c-article-table" data-test="inline-table" data-container-section="table" id="table-5"><figure><figcaption class="c-article-table__figcaption"><b id="Tab5" data-test="table-caption">Table 5.5 Change in the level of risk of wildfire within the framework of three development scenarios until 2031</b></figcaption><div class="u-text-right u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="table-link" data-track="click" data-track-action="view table" data-track-label="button" rel="nofollow" href="/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-56089-7_5/tables/5" aria-label="Full size table 5"><span>Full size table</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div><p>In the period until 2031, the unfavourable demographic processes are not expected to change significantly, apart from the ID scenario. Given that all scenarios include infrastructural development, which should counteract the consequences of population concentration in the coastal zone, depopulation in other zones and the aged population structure overall, the wildfire risk remains the same from the demographic point of view. The exception is the ID scenario, where the more favourable population dynamics and structure, especially in better accessible areas, is expected to decrease the wildfire incidence in all three zones.</p><p>With regard to economic activities and land use, the wildfire incidence remains unchanged in the littoral zone for all scenarios. In the MoT scenario, it is expected to increase in the hinterland and on the islands due to the overall lack of advancements in sectors other than tourism and underutilisation of spatial resources. The ST and ID scenarios bring a decrease in the level of wildfire risk in the island and hinterland zones due to a more balanced economic development and more sustainable use of resources.</p><p>In the case of climate change, the wildfire incidence is expected to depend on the general development rationale and institutional framework. In the littoral, there is no significant change in the wildfire incidence across all scenarios. In the ST scenario, with a stronger institutional framework that counteracts the level of risk generally increased by climate change, the wildfire incidence remains the same for the other two zones as well. In the MoT scenario, wildfire incidence could increase for islands and the hinterland because of the weaker institutional response. It is the opposite in the ID scenario, where a strong institutional framework supports the overall integral development, which should attribute to a lower wildfire incidence.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Conclusion"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec10-section"><h2 id="Sec10" class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">5.6 </span>Conclusion</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec10-content"><p>The differences in fire risk resulting from the prevalence of fire-prone vegetation between the case study areas are already evident in the nineteenth century. The island of Vis has the highest proportion of land exposed to high fire risk compared to the other two study areas in the coastal and inland areas, where fire risk is medium.</p><p>Throughout the twentieth century, a decrease in the total (agricultural) population and the decline in traditional agricultural activity have been observed not only in Croatia but also in other parts of the Mediterranean. These processes, coupled with littoralisation and abandonment of pastoralism, have been identified as contributing factors to the increase in forest fire risk and changes in fire regime and behaviour, with an increase in larger and more intense fires.<sup><a href="#Fn81"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>81</a></sup> Our statistical analysis of land cover changes confirmed that the increased fire risk is mainly due to the homogenisation of land cover in terms of the prevalence of maquis and scrubland, the most fire-prone vegetation types, at the expense of abandoned pastures, which has led to an increase in highly flammable fuels.</p><p>As a result, the fire risk has increased dramatically in all three socio-environmental zones. High risk is absolutely prevalent in all zones, exceeding 92% on Vis island. However, the increase in high risk since the nineteenth century has been highest in the littoral zone, where it increased from 8.7% to over 70% of the study area.</p><p>The analysis has also shown that the increase in temperature and decrease in precipitation—which typically contribute to an elevated risk of fire—were not significant factors in the observed increase in fire risk in the Croatian Dinaric Karst. This is because the climate parameters were already at the highest category of fire risk assessment in the nineteenth century. However, it is important to note that the continuation of current socio-economic processes, combined with the already observed and predicted effects of climate change in the Mediterranean region (such as higher temperatures and longer droughts in summer), could contribute to an increase in the frequency of forest fires in the future. The wildland–urban interface has been identified as a potential new fire risk area due to the accumulation of fuel and the increase in peri-urban and recreational activities. However, in the development scenarios, the littoral zone is predicted to have a consistent (unchanged) wildfire incidence, mainly due to better infrastructure development and institutional support. Out of the three possible development scenarios, tourism monoculture proves to be the most likely to increase the risk of forest fires, whilst the integral development scenario and (slightly less) the sustainable tourism scenario would lead to a reduction in fire risk in both the hinterland and littoral zones of the Dinaric Karst.</p></div></div></section>
